title: Insurable-at-Closing: Pay-on-Closing Insurability Sheets for WUI Listings
one_liner: Listing agents order a 48-hour parcel evidence and carrier-routing sheet before a wildfire-zone home goes to market, and the seller pays a flat fee at closing only if the sale closes.
customer: Listing agents and brokerages selling wildland-urban-interface homes in Front Range and mountain markets such as the Boulder foothills, Evergreen and Conifer, Estes Park, Black Forest and the Colorado Springs foothills. Title and escrow officers are the channel, and the seller pays through the settlement statement. A licensed WUI-specialist independent agency is the placement partner.
problem: A lender will not close without a bound homeowners policy. In WUI sales the bind often fails late: the buyer's quote is declined on a score cutoff and the contract clock is running. Neither the seller's nor the buyer's agent can say in advance which carriers will write the lot. No statute helps at that point, because the new-business decline is not a nonrenewal appeal. Free homeowner appeal kits do not touch this moment.
solution: When the home is listed, the agent orders an Insurability Sheet. It is a one-page PDF and a data file with a lot condition ledger from dated imagery and lidar, a ranked list of pre-closing fixes with cost and time to complete, and a carrier route showing which carriers' models see this lot accurately and have a human exception path. The partner agency supplies indicative appetite and quotes. At contract, buyers' agents can re-run the sheet in 24 hours. The lot evidence goes to underwriters as an exception referral at carriers that read it, and away from carriers using coarse 30 m models that will decline the same lot on a raster.
why_now: Colorado WUI homeowners' rates roughly doubled in 2020-2025 (per the parent research) and carriers keep retreating, so insurance availability is now a closing risk. HB25-1182 disclosures mean sellers can now hold a score but not a plan. Cheap high-resolution archives make a 48-hour turnaround affordable. I could not verify local closing-fall-through statistics or new pre-listing tools in this pass, so check both first.
revenue_model: A $395 flat fee on the settlement statement, due only if the sale closes; $150 upfront if the agent prefers. A $75 rapid re-run for buyer-side agents. A placement technology fee or revenue share from the partner agency on policies bound (about 10-15% commission on roughly $5k premiums, renewing yearly), structured with counsel around RESPA and producer-compensation rules. At 8% of roughly 6,000 annual WUI sales in the five focus counties, that is about $0.2M in fees in year one. Expanding across the Western WUI markets lifts this to the low tens of millions.
non_obvious_insight: The same lot gets very different treatment from different carriers. The parent research cites identical Class A homes receiving discounts of 0.7%, 12% and 41%. That suggests the profitable move is routing the lot to the carrier whose model sees it correctly, and not rebutting a score. Routing needs no statutory appeal right, so it works in California, Oregon and Washington where the Colorado law does not apply. The moat is a bindability database of carrier appetite by parcel features and actual bind outcomes. Score vendors see scores, not who binds, and agents see only their own quotes.
first_30_days: Sign one Front Range WUI-specialist independent agency as the licensed placement partner. Recruit 2 title or escrow offices and 5 listing agents. Run 20 listings with the fee contingent on closing and track policy-bound-before-closing rate, days saved and deals rescued. Get a written RESPA and producer-compensation review before any fee reaches a bank account. Turn the results into one case study for brokerage sales meetings.
lineage: mutation of I1148 ('Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery. | How this version avoids them: FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score serve homeowners disputing an existing score and have nothing for the sale moment or for carrier routing. IBHS and Wildfire Partners are on-site programs that take weeks, and they do not fit a 30-day contract, though they could later validate a sheet. Road Home Exteriors sells evidence with hardening jobs, not before a sale. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk score for carriers and do not see the buyer's bind attempt. Possible new rivals are quote-at-offer tools and portals with climate scores; they quote from their own models with no lot evidence and no multi-carrier routing. I could not check for those in this pass.

title: Plug-or-Pitch: Turning Idle Wells Into Assets
one_liner: Screen idle and orphan oil wells for hydrogen, helium and heat evidence, and get paid a share of the plugging liability that disappears when a well is transferred to an explorer who wants a ready-made hole to the basement.
customer: The payer is the liability holder, not the explorer. Wedge: independent operators in Kansas and Oklahoma holding 50-500 idle, shut-in or temporarily abandoned wells under rising plugging and bonding pressure. Phase 2: state orphan-well programs (funded by the $4.7B IIJA orphan-well money) and state land offices. The other side of the transaction, who takes the well and pays a placement fee, is a hydrogen, helium or geothermal junior that today drills new holes at seven-figure cost.
problem: An idle well is a negative asset: plugging often costs tens of thousands of dollars per well (an estimate to confirm state by state), and operators or states carry that liability for years. Meanwhile the parent idea's buyers spend roughly seven figures to drill a test hole to basement, and a wellbore that already penetrates basement, with a file that shows non-flammable gas or elevated temperature, is worth many multiples of its plugging cost to them. The two sides never find each other because the evidence sits in scanned well files, and juniors in the parent's research 'do not budget $15-50k a year for data' but do budget hard money for holes. Price anchored to a known plugging cost is a much easier sale than price anchored to speculative exploration value.
solution: A per-well 'Reuse Dossier' built from each idle well's own file and its offsets: hydrogen/helium/N2-rich gas shows from mud logs, DSTs and driller notes, depth to basement, casing/cement/plugging status, bottom-hole temperature and gradient, and produced-water chemistry, each with page-image provenance and a confidence grade. A Reuse Score estimates re-entry cost against new-drill cost and states the single test that would confirm the lead. Wells are bundled into small re-entry lots and placed with repurposers under a recorded assignment of plugging liability (with state transfer approval and financial assurance), often keeping a retained royalty or carry for the seller. The operator pays nothing upfront: screening is free and the startup is paid from the avoided liability and from the placement. Geothermal scoring can be sourced from partners such as WellScout AI rather than built.
why_now: State and federal pressure on idle wells is at its peak: IIJA orphan-well plugging money is flowing through the late 2020s, and states have built lists that did not exist five years ago. Hydrogen and helium juniors raised $20M-$245M rounds (Koloma, Terra AI, Mantle8) and HyTerra proved that twinning historic wells works, so demand for cheap access to basement-penetrating holes is real. VLM extraction cost per well file has collapsed to a few dollars, which makes free screening for an operator affordable on a contingency basis; that would have been uneconomic in 2022.
revenue_model: Contingent success fee of about 15% of the avoided plugging cost (from the operator or state) when a well transfers, plus a $10-25k placement fee (or 5% of any bonus or sale price) from the repurposer, plus $500-1,500 for a premium dossier and a $10-25k/year 'reuse lot' feed for juniors. Illustrative unit economics: an operator with 200 idle wells costs about $16k to screen (about $80/well compute plus geologist review); if 1-2% clear the bar (1-2 wells above the 0.5% Paris Basin rate is plausible for a targeted fairway) and each saves about $40k of plugging cost, revenue is $6-12k in liability fees plus placement fees per portfolio, and a state program is 10-50x that. The wedge is deliberately contingent so the customer has no downside.
non_obvious_insight: The bid-ask spread has the wrong sign: the holder sees a negative asset (minus the plugging cost) and the explorer sees a hole worth a multiple of its plugging cost, and the only missing ingredient is verified evidence about which wells sit on the positive side. Low hit rate (about 0.5% in the Paris Basin study) kills a subscription atlas but not a contingency screen, because the operator's cost is zero and one hit pays for the portfolio. The startup's true asset is not the data but the transferable, state-approved playbook for liability assignment plus a book of buyers, which creates a two-sided market that data vendors and free datasets cannot replicate.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the public inactive/TA well lists from the Kansas KCC and Oklahoma OCC and pick 300 wells that reach basement in the Nemaha corridor. Week 2: extract their files and offsets and produce 30 Reuse Dossiers with a scored top 10. Week 3: call 25 independent operators and the plugging-fund manager at one state agency with the offer 'give us your 100 worst idle wells, screening is free, we take 15% of the avoided plugging cost if we place a well'. In parallel get 2-3 juniors to sign non-binding LOIs to consider re-entry lots. Week 4: sign 3 contingency agreements and confirm with the state regulator what transfer-with-assumption of liability requires. Before building further, run 15 calls to check the two unverified assumptions: state transfer rules and re-entry cost versus a new drill.
lineage: mutation of I1085 ('Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. The Paris Basin OCR study found only 26 wells with H2 detection out of about 5,000 in the database (0.5%), which suggests few real leads per basin. Unserved specifics: (1) the 20-30 state and provincial archives whose scans are not yet digitized, with a defensible per-record confidence grade (sampling method, air contamination, analytical era); (2) one integrated He, H2 and heat layer, where the players found each cover a single commodity; (3) delivery to small juniors, landmen and lease advisors who cannot fund in-house teams. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side. | How this version avoids them: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR and GeoMap: free datasets give regional or aggregate layers, none identifies which specific idle well is a transferable reuse candidate, so they are our inputs, not substitutes. WellScout AI is the closest overlap (screens oil wells for geothermal conversion); it covers only heat and sells software to operators, so we can partner on thermal scoring and win on multi-commodity gas evidence plus the transaction. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar keep their data in-house and are demand-side buyers of re-entry lots, not rivals. NthDS and Enverus/TGS sell files to buyers of O&G data; they do not take contingent fees on liability transfers and have channel conflict doing so. AKAP, Wood Mackenzie and Rystad sell market intelligence, not well-level transactions. Not covered in the parent's research and to be verified: oil-and-gas A&D brokers and state orphan-well reuse pilots.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. (3) The GitHub search for open-source tools found nothing relevant. Unverified, from background knowledge: engineering and rate consultancies (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen and similar) do apparent-loss audits and revenue-protection reviews on a fee basis. Contract meter-testing firms and meter distributors run large-meter testing and right-sizing programs, usually to sell replacement meters. Small local billing-audit shops may exist. Genuinely unserved: an independent, outcome-priced screen of large-account meter accuracy that ranks specific accounts by expected dollars using consumption history, and that does not depend on one meter vendor's hardware. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive.

title: Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families
one_liner: A flat-fee, advocate-supervised 'estate file' service that gets a dead parent's or grandfather's land, shares and dormant accounts legally transferred, sold to the adult children who pay from Nairobi, Dallas or Dubai.
customer: Salaried urban and diaspora Kenyans aged 30-55 whose rural parents or grandparents died (or are old) with land still registered in a dead person's name. They pay from abroad or from the city. A secondary B2B payer is any SACCO, coop or bank that needs cleared successions before it releases deposits or lends against land.
problem: Most rural family land is still titled to a dead grandfather or father because nobody completed succession. The process needs a chief's letter, a death certificate, consents from every heir, gazettement, a wait before confirmation of grant, and then transmission at the land registry, which is often 1-3 years and many trips. Until it is done the land cannot be leased, mortgaged, subdivided or cleanly sold, siblings fight, and the deceased's SACCO deposits, coop shares, insurance and pension sit unclaimed. The real blocker is coordinating 8 to 20 relatives to sign, not the court.
solution: Wedge product is a 'Family Estate Map' for roughly KES 15-25k (pricing to be tested). The child sends photos of the title, IDs, death certificate and old share certificates over WhatsApp. An LLM pipeline extracts names and parcel numbers, handles the multiple-name and spelling-variant problem in Kenyan naming, builds the family tree and likely heirs, and lists the consents needed. It runs official land searches and asset-discovery letters to SACCOs, coops, insurers and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, then outputs a court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits. A home-county field agent collects the chief's letter and relatives' signatures or thumbprints, with video proof of consent. Partner advocates then file and shepherd the case at their own scale fees. Later upsells are surveyor subdivision and lease or loan readiness.
why_now: The generation that took up land in the 1960s-80s through settlement schemes and land-buying companies is dying now, so the succession backlog is peaking. Diaspora remittances are near record levels (roughly US$5bn a year), and families increasingly ask 'sort out the land' rather than 'build a house'. Digitised land records (Ardhisasa) and court e-filing reduce physical running, though their current coverage needs checking. LLMs can now read messy scanned title and ID documents and draft forms in English while chatting with clients in Swahili. I could not run live searches, so verify current UFAA agent rules, court e-filing scope for successions, and fee schedules before building.
revenue_model: Flat fee per estate file, paid by M-Pesa or card from abroad. Advocate fees are billed by the advocates themselves, so the company sells software and case management and does not split fees with non-lawyers. Asset discovery is a flat add-on fee, not a percentage cut of UFAA payouts, because UFAA discourages middlemen taking a share. B2B revenue is per cleaned member estate from SACCOs and coops. Later there is referral income from surveyors and land-backed lenders once titles are clean.
non_obvious_insight: Rural Kenya's biggest pool of unused collateral is land trapped in the name of the dead. The bottleneck is family coordination and evidence gathering, so the product is a coordination workflow sold to the sibling who has money and guilt, not a land registry or a lawyer marketplace. VCs looking at land-tech miss that the payer is the diaspora child, not the farmer.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Murang'a or Kakamega) and recruit two advocates who already do succession work. Build intake on WhatsApp Business, Airtable and an LLM extraction script. Sell 10 files at a pilot discount through your own family network, church and alumni groups, and diaspora WhatsApp and Facebook groups such as Kenyans in Texas or the UK. Publish a free 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' checker as lead-gen. Track days from intake to gazettement as the core metric.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them.

title: Cavity ID: Tool-of-Origin Evidence via Counsel
one_liner: Expert-grade 'which tool made this part, and when' reports, built from parts the brand already holds in the US and sold through China-facing IP law firms to brands whose ex-supplier is selling their product.
customer: Wedge: branded hard-goods companies ($10M-$150M revenue: housewares, pet, fitness, hand tools, juvenile, small appliances) that sell injection-molded or die-cast products on Amazon/Walmart/Target, hold a design patent, trade dress or registered mark on the part, and ended a China supplier in the last 18 months. Buyer of record is their outside China/IP counsel (15-25 boutique cross-border firms), who engage us as a consulting expert so the work is privileged. The brand's GC or COO signs off on the disbursement.
problem: The brand sees look-alike units of its own product on Amazon, Temu and 1688 at 30% below its price, and suspects the ex-supplier is running its steel on a third shift. Today its lawyers can send a cease-and-desist built on suspicion, and the supplier answers 'that is a copy, not ours'. Marketplace takedown vendors produce screenshots and listings, not proof of which tool made the part or that it was made after the orders stopped. Without that proof the brand loses the negotiation over tool release, and losing it costs six or seven figures in tooling and margin.
solution: One product, the Tool-of-Origin Report, with no China operations and no extraction business. (1) Baseline: macro-image 30-60 retained parts per SKU, taken from the brand's own US inventory, returns and QA samples across different lots and dates. Build a cavity signature library (cavity ID marks, gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, parting-line and texture flaws) plus a wear-over-time curve, since tool wear is monotonic and dates the tool's state. (2) Attribution: test-buy 5-10 suspect units, match them to a cavity and tool state, and report a forensic-style likelihood ratio, including whether the tool state postdates the last PO. (3) Counsel-ready pack: chain of custody, methodology and a signed declaration from a retained independent molding-process engineer, formatted for the Amazon Report-a-Violation and APEX flows, the Alibaba IP platform, CBP recordation, a demand letter or litigation. Monitoring is bought or white-labeled from an existing vendor. Field capture in China is subcontracted, and only in a later pre-exit 'baseline while the supplier is still cooperative' tier.
why_now: The 2025 tariff whiplash and the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling (per the parent research) have produced a wave of supplier breakups. Formal-entry bulk imports rose after the end of the US de minimis exemption in 2025, which makes overrun sellers easier to reach through CBP and marketplaces. Cheap macro-imaging plus modern vision models make tool-mark statistics feasible at SMB prices, where a forensic lab used to cost $30k+ per case.
revenue_model: Baseline $4,500 per product family. Test-buy attribution report $6,500 per case (up to 10 samples). Expert declaration or testimony $350/hr through counsel. Optional 'Overrun Watch' retainer $1,500/month per family, with two attributions a year included and monitoring white-labeled. Counsel buys the report as a disbursement and marks it up under its own billing, so there are no referral fees, which avoids fee-sharing ethics problems. Target 60 clients at about $14k blended annual spend, roughly $0.85M ARR, by month 12. Gross margin about 65% (assumption). Bottom-up reachable market is roughly 1,500 qualifying brands (assumption to validate).
non_obvious_insight: The evidence a lawyer needs is not 'this is a copy'. It is 'this was made on your steel after you stopped ordering'. Tool wear is a clock: edges round, texture erodes, flash grows, and repairs leave dated marks. So parts you already own in a US warehouse from 2022, 2024 and 2025 reconstruct the wear timeline without ever visiting China. Routing the work through counsel also makes it privileged, and it moves the spend from a marketing or brand-protection budget to a legal-dispute budget that is bigger and less price-sensitive.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: interview 12 China-facing IP lawyers and 8 GCs, asking what evidence they wish they had at the demand-letter stage and whether they would buy at $6.5k. In parallel, run a blind validation. Buy multi-cavity molded parts from known sources across 2-3 tool states and test whether our imaging plus statistics assigns cavity and tool state correctly (target above 95%). Publish the methodology memo. Retain one independent molding-process engineer as expert of record. Weeks 3-4: sell 3 paid $2,500 Overrun Audits (test-buys plus a one-page verdict), qualified on the client owning enforceable IP on the part, through one law-firm co-marketing partner. Kill signal: fewer than 3 of 12 lawyers say they would buy, or blind accuracy below 90%.
lineage: mutation of I0552 ('Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. title: The True Acceptance Map for Rural Transfers
one_liner: Voice AI agents call every receiving psychiatric unit and specialty hospital each night to learn what they will actually accept, and rural ERs text a number to find out who will say yes.
customer: Critical access hospital EDs, state hospital associations and state rural health offices (paid with Rural Health Transformation Program funds), and state behavioral health authorities. Subscription per hospital or per state.
problem: A rural ER holding a suicidal 16-year-old, or a stroke, trauma or OB patient, may spend 3-8 hours making phone calls to place them. State bed registries say beds are open, but the real decision is made by a house supervisor at 2am applying unwritten rules: no IV drug history, no one-to-one sitter, no autism, no patients over 250 lb, no out-of-state Medicaid, no aggression, and no calls after 9pm without a physician-to-physician call. Every ER charge nurse keeps a battered binder or a phone note of who says yes to what and who to ask for. It lives in one head, and it goes out of date when a house supervisor changes.
solution: Use voice agents to call each facility's intake line on a schedule and extract structured, current answers: true open capacity by population, unwritten exclusions, insurance rules, the name and direct number of the person who decides, and the hours that person answers. Serve it back through a plain SMS interface. A nurse texts 'psych, 16yo, Medicaid, sitter needed, hx cutting' and gets a ranked call list with the exact script to use (the words that get an acceptance). Only facility rules are collected. No patient data is ever in the calls. Later, sell a receiving-side listing so facilities can pre-qualify referrals and get fewer dead-end calls.
why_now: Every state has now posted Rural Health Transformation Program funding opportunities (as of August 2026), and care coordination and access technology are core uses. Research on bed-tracking systems shows registries still leave clinicians phoning to check appropriateness, especially for aggressive, medically complex, autistic and dementia patients. Voice agents from 2025-26 can now hold a natural two-minute call with an intake nurse for a few cents. The workforce shortage means intake lines are answered by fewer people, which makes the tacit rules more valuable.
revenue_model: $300-600 per ER per month for SMS access. State-level licenses of $100-300k per year paid from RHTP or behavioral health funds. A second line is a receiving-facility listing at about $500 per month per facility. The proprietary asset is a data graph of real rules that no registry has.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable data is not bed counts, which are wrong within an hour. It is the tacit acceptance criteria and the identity of the human who decides, and it can only be learned by phone at night. That is why bed-registry vendors (built on hospital self-reporting) miss it. Facilities that discover their rules are being published accurately will cooperate, because a dead-end call costs them time too.
first_30_days: Pick one state or region. Type up the founder nurse's own binder, about 60-80 facilities, into a spreadsheet. Wire an off-the-shelf voice agent platform to call each facility nightly and write results to a table. Put an SMS bot in front of it with a Twilio number. Give it free to five ERs in the region and compare call counts and time to placement before and after. Bring the numbers to the state hospital association and the RHTP office.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: OpenBeds (Bamboo Health, formerly Appriss Health), Behavioral Health Link (GCAL Real-Time Bed Registry and Crisis Now platform), State and hospital-association psychiatric bed registries (NC BH SCAN, WHA Psychiatric Bed Locator, Minnesota Bed Tracker, MABHA, Michigan registry dashboard), Human placement and crisis-access services (Illinois CARES Line, Massachusetts EPIA protocol, regional psychiatric emergency services, telepsychiatry vendors such as Array Behavioral Care and Access TeleCare). White space: Nobody found does the specific thing. Across roughly 20 searches, no startup, product, or open-source tool uses voice agents to phone receiving psychiatric units and specialty hospitals on a schedule and record their tacit acceptance rules, the name and hours of the decision-maker, and the script that works. The unserved wedge is real but narrow. (1) Registries (OpenBeds, BHL, state portals) capture bed counts and formal criteria through facility self-report. The 2019 ASPE and Psychiatric Services work found no state registry linked to EHR or ADT data, and respondents rated registry accuracy and timeliness poor. Only NC has hourly automation, and that is bed count, not rule extraction. (2) Nobody delivers a ranked call list plus script by SMS to a rural ER charge nurse. Registries are portals that still end in 'call the facility'. (3) The hardest-to-place groups are children, autism and IDD, aggression, medically complex, out-of-state Medicaid. Boarding research shows these patients wait longest, and generic registry filters handle them worst. (4) Decline reasons and real decision-makers are not aggregated across facilities anywhere. Not unserved: bed availability, digital referrals, and generic outbound voice AI. Also not a clean white space: stroke, trauma and OB, where hospital-run transfer centers and TeleTracking, Central Logic and RelateCare already own the workflow.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.

title: Contingency Spread Recovery for Public Benefit Pools
one_liner: Zero-upfront PBM pass-through audits sold to school and local-government benefit pools, paid as a share of verified savings, using a shadow pharmacy price list built from local independents' remits, with a slice of each fee paid back to those pharmacies.
customer: Executive directors and boards of multi-employer public benefit pools: school-district benefit trusts and joint powers authorities, county-association and municipal-league health trusts, with 5,000-100,000 lives across dozens of member entities. They buy once for many districts, are subject to open-records and audit pressure, and carry political risk if a PBM overcharge surfaces. Secondary: single counties or districts of 300-3,000 lives (free pilot tier). Payer is the pool, only when savings are verified. No PBM ever pays us.
problem: A pool pays its PBM a billed price per NDC per claim, and its contract may promise pass-through, lowest-of pricing or audit rights. It cannot see what the PBM paid the pharmacy, so the audit rights only test billing against the PBM's own data. Consultants either charge flat fees on PBM-supplied files or are compensated in part by carriers and PBMs (disclosure of broker and consultant compensation is now required under the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, though disclosure is not independence). Local officials also watch the town's last pharmacy close while the same PBM underpays it. The old obstacle was a claim-level join needing consent from both sides, which is why the parent's tie-out looked hard.
solution: (1) Shadow price list: 20-40 in-region independents contribute NDC-level paid unit price, fill date and BIN/PCN/group only (no patient identifiers), extracted locally. The team reconstructs, by week, what the PBM's retail network actually pays per NDC for the top 200-300 generics that drive most retail generic spend. (2) Tie-out to any plan: take the pool's own claims file (via contractual audit right or public-records request) and compare billed unit price per NDC and date to the reconstructed pharmacy-paid price, producing a spread per member per month by drug. The pharmacies never need to have filled that plan's claims, because a network's pharmacy MAC is common across clients. Scope is stated honestly as retail, and mail and specialty are excluded unless data exists. (3) Screen first: only take pools whose contracts promise pass-through or lowest-of pricing, or who will run an RFP; ordinary legal spread contracts yield renegotiation, not breach recovery. (4) Act: audit-rights letter, renegotiation, or an RFP among 3-5 bidders including the Big 3 and transparent PBMs. (5) Optional Local Access Rider: the pool redirects about 20% of verified savings into a per-Rx access fee paid to in-county independents, a plan-design choice that keeps pharmacies alive and makes them allies. Savings are verified by replaying 12 months post-change against the same shadow list, with a cap.
why_now: Local officials have political will after Rite Aid's exit and Walgreens' closures. Fiduciary and open-records pressure on PBM spend is rising, transparent PBMs give pools credible switch destinations, and federal and state reporting mandates create a paper trail to check (verify current scope). LLM and OCR parsing makes contributing remits a one-day task. January renewals also drive RFP timing, and pools' boards typically decide in Q4-Q1.
revenue_model: Contingency of 12-15% of first-year verified savings, with a floor for pools over 10,000 lives. Illustrative: a 20,000-life pool spends roughly $25-30M a year on drugs; a 4-8% price gap is $1-2M and a 12% share is $120-240k. Recurring Pass-Through Monitor after the audit at about $0.30-0.40 per member per month ($70-95k a year for 20,000 lives). Data co-op dividend: 15-20% of fees paid to contributing pharmacies pro rata as a fair-market-value data license (never tied to referrals; structure with counsel, and keep it away from any federal program business). A few hundred such pools nationally make this a $30M-100M revenue niche.
non_obvious_insight: The employer does not need the claims the pharmacies saw. A PBM's retail pharmacy price list is common across clients in a network tier, so a crowd of pharmacies can reconstruct the hidden list once and any plan's billed prices can be compared to it. That turns a two-party consent-and-join problem into a price-list problem, and each additional pool costs almost nothing to audit. Contingency plus zero PBM money creates the only auditor with clean hands in a field where advisors are paid by the counterparties. Public bodies can compel data that private employers cannot, and the Local Access Rider turns the pharmacies from data suppliers into political allies.
first_30_days: Pick one state with many independents and public pools. Days 1-10: recruit 20 pharmacies through the state association, offering a free margin report in exchange for NDC-level price extracts; build the shadow list for the top 200 generics. Days 10-25: offer one county or district (300-3,000 lives) a free pilot, obtain its claims file by consent or open-records request, and produce a one-page spread letter with a dollars-per-member figure. Days 20-30: take the letter to a pool's executive director and broker and negotiate a contingency letter agreement (12% of verified savings, no fee if zero). Hire a healthcare attorney for data-license and dividend terms. Kill criterion: the pilot shows under 2% spread on retail generics, or fewer than 12 pharmacies agree to contribute.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:

A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.

title: Stack-Pooled 24/7 Article 14 Desk for Non-EU Brands
one_liner: A guaranteed-SLA Assigned Representative that files CRA Article 14 reports for 50-250 person non-EU connected-device brands, doing the triage once per shared component stack (Tuya, ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek) and fanning it out to every client on that stack.
customer: Medium-sized (50-250 staff, above the small-enterprise fine exemption) non-EU smart-home, e-mobility and networking brands based in Shenzhen, Taiwan, Korea and the US that sell into the EU via Amazon EU and retail. Their firmware comes from an ODM on one of 3 shared stacks: Tuya/Matter modules, ESP-IDF/ESP32, or OpenWrt/Realtek SDKs. The buyer is the head of product or compliance; the introduction comes through the EU Responsible Person/EPR (WEEE and packaging) service providers who already serve these sellers.
problem: These brands do not know what is inside their own firmware because the ODM built it, so they cannot tell whether a KEV/EUVD entry hits them. They have no one awake in Europe at 3am Sunday to decide 'actively exploited, affects us, file'. The 72h and 14-day clocks carry fines even if the 24h clock does not, and their EU retail partners will start asking for proof of process. Existing options each miss part of this. Software (CVD Portal, CRACI, Regulus) stops at timers and drafts, with filing left to the customer. Finite State and H-X draft notices but leave filing to the customer. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 or price. EcoComply is an AR mandate with no triage.
solution: Three things in one contract. (1) Named-analyst AR mandate plus a written SLA: triage decision within 4h and early warning filed inside 24h, weekends included, under a client-approved decision tree and pre-authorised actions. (2) Stack-pooled triage: a stack owner analyses each exploited entry once against the stack's component graph and issues per-firmware-version pre-approved VEX and notice drafts to every enrolled brand on that stack, so a client-named analyst only checks the version delta and files. (3) Firmware-fingerprint onboarding: the brand uploads a firmware image or OTA URL and the desk builds the component list itself, removing the missing-SBOM problem. Every KEV/EUVD entry also gets a timestamped per-product 'affected / not affected' decision, delivered monthly as a signed monitoring evidence log. That log is the recurring deliverable when nothing was exploited, and it is what retailers and market surveillance authorities will ask for. The 24h and 72h drills run on the client's own stack.
why_now: Article 14 reporting went live on 11 Sep 2026 (about 18 days ago) and the ENISA SRP opened the same day. Patchstack shows managed filing is now legal and being productised, so the window before it becomes a checkbox is roughly 6-12 months. Retail supplier manuals are being rewritten for the Dec 2027 full application, and GPSR (since Dec 2024) already trained these sellers to buy EU-representative services.
revenue_model: Base fee of about EUR 3.6-4.8k per year per product family (AR mandate, stack monitoring, monthly evidence log, one drill), well above EcoComply's EUR 1.5k AR-only anchor but below a monthly PSIRT retainer. Filing events cost EUR 1.5-3k each. Tabletop drills and 'clock audit' are EUR 1.5-5k. Wholesale white-label 24/7 back-end capacity is sold to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and SBOM platforms. Target is 100 product families by month 12 (about EUR 400k ARR). One stack analyst covering 30-100 clients keeps gross margin above 65%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not filing, it is the stack-to-firmware truth table. Brands do not know what is inside, but the desk sees which SDK forks and versions actually ship across dozens of brands. That is a cornered resource that a one-off consultancy cannot copy: each new client on a stack has near-zero marginal analyst cost and improves the fingerprint coverage. Also, 95% of what the desk produces is 'not affected'. Selling signed negative evidence as the monthly deliverable fixes the judges' 'insurance nobody buys until audited' flaw. Targeting 50-250 person firms sidesteps the Art 64(10) small-enterprise exemption on the 24h fine.
first_30_days: Week 1: get a professional-indemnity quote, and get written confirmation from ENISA or a national CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts. Get counsel to settle how the 24h clock starts when the desk detects first, and draft the AR mandate and decision tree. Weeks 1-2: build component graphs for 3 stacks (ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek, Tuya) covering the top 25 exploited component families of the last 24 months, using open-source firmware unpacking such as EMBA. Weeks 2-4: sell a EUR 1.5k '24h drill + firmware fingerprint' to 20 brands sourced from 3 EPR/GPSR representative providers and Amazon-EU seller communities. The drill simulates an exploited entry hitting their stack and measures their real time-to-decision. Convert 5 into annual AR+desk contracts. Contract 3 part-time named analysts across time zones and confirm the SRP login rules apply to them.

- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: It refuses the generic 'PSIRT retainer' frame owned by TridentSec, Finite State and Cybellum. It sells the one thing they call customer-owned, which is a contractually guaranteed filing as the named AR. It uses the SBOM and monitoring layer (CVD Portal at EUR 99/mo, CRACI, Zealience, ONEKEY) as commodity input rather than product. It is aimed at non-EU mid-size brands, which Cybellum's enterprise focus and Patchstack's free open-source-only service do not serve. Its economics come from pooling by stack, which per-client consultancies and per-seat platforms cannot match. Incumbent MSSPs and certification bodies (Kudelski, TUV SUD, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas) become white-label distributors rather than rivals, since the desk offers them the back end they lack.

title: Independent Herd Audits for Loan Participation Buyers
one_liner: Charge the correspondent banks, credit unions and credit funds that buy pieces of cattle loans they cannot see, using sampling audits and a verified collateral tape sold through bankers' banks.
customer: The participation desk or chief credit officer at correspondent ag banks, credit unions and ag-focused credit funds that buy participations in cattle loans from community banks. Community banks hit legal lending limits and sell off big pieces of $2M+ herd loans. Channel partners are the bankers' banks that broker those participations. Later buyers are pool purchasers such as Farmer Mac-style secondary-market programs.
problem: A participant that owns 80-90% of a cattle loan has never seen the cattle. It relies on the lead bank's annual inspection, and the lead bank has already sold most of the risk, keeps servicing fees and has reason to want the loan to look clean. Participation agreements normally give buyers information and inspection rights, but the rights go unused because sending an inspector to a ranch two states away costs $1,500+ and buyers do not know how to audit a herd. The parent's fraud case (about $2.8M against 850 head, claimed and unverified) sits in the loan size that small banks typically participate out. That is a hypothesis to confirm.
solution: A 'Participation Audit' program sold to the buyer of risk, not the originator. Tier 1 desk audit ($300-500): a document reconciliation (sale-barn and brand records, tag and vet purchases) plus a lien search, compared against the lead bank's inspection report. Tier 2 ($1,200-2,000): adds a vet-attested chute-side scan or a credentialed field inspector, with geotagged photos and an EID or visual tag scan, timed to preg-check, weaning or a scheduled sale. Tier 3: surprise audit triggered by a lead-bank downgrade, a delinquency or a cattle-price drop. Buyers audit a random 15-25% of each pool every year, so every borrower knows the draw could land on them, which deters fraud. Buyers also get a verified collateral tape with loan-level fields (head, class, pregnancy rate, variance, lien position, date). That tape lets them price participations and lets funds bid for them. Bankers' banks embed the service in their participation platform for a 20-25% revenue share.
why_now: Herd rebuilding is debt-financed, so more cattle loans are being participated, and delinquencies are rising. A cattle-fraud headline (claimed in the parent, unverified) makes participants ask why they trust the lead bank's word. Examiner guidance generally expects participants to do their own credit analysis rather than lean on the lead, which is worth confirming with counsel. Non-bank capital has been moving into ag credit and needs diligence infrastructure. Remote document reconciliation makes a $400 Tier 1 audit profitable, where a field-only inspector could never be. Farm-loan stress typically creates an appetite for independent verification.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees: Tier 1 at about $400 and Tier 2 at about $1,500. Add $250/loan/year of monitoring, plus a 20-25% share to the bankers' bank. Data subscription for the verified collateral tape at $2-5K/month per buyer. Later, a 5-10 bps diligence fee on pool trades. Example: a correspondent buyer holding $150M across 150 cattle loans pays 150 x $400 + 38 Tier 2 audits x $1,500 + 150 x $250 = about $155K/yr. Ten such buyers is roughly $1.5M in recurring revenue. Field inspection labor is variable, using vet and tech partners paid per visit.
non_obvious_insight: In a participation, the party with the most money at risk has the least information and holds a contractual right that nobody uses because exercising it is operationally impossible. The buyer's question is not 'is the borrower honest' but 'is my lead bank's report honest'. Independence from the lead bank is therefore the product, and adverse selection disappears because the buyer picks the sample after buying, and randomness is the deterrent. Vets are optional at Tier 2, so vet reluctance no longer blocks the business.
first_30_days: Call 15 people: 5 bankers' banks and correspondent participation desks, 5 community-bank lead lenders that sell cattle participations, and 5 credit unions that buy them. Ask for the inspection clause in an actual participation agreement, whether anyone has ever inspected a participated cattle loan, who did it and what it cost. Find one buyer willing to pay $1,000 each for 5 participated cattle loans and invoke its inspection rights with the lead bank. Time the visits to fall preg-check or weaning days with two partner vets or field inspectors. Deliver five Tier 2 reports and a one-page comparison of what we found against the lead bank's file. Use that comparison to pitch a bankers' bank on adding the program to its participation platform.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.
