- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. | How this version avoids them: None of the eight researched vendors (CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/Beef Passport, Merck/Allflex/Vence, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg, Gallagher) sells to the buyer of risk, and none can, because their paying customer is the producer being audited. IMI verifies claims for marketing programs. Our payer, our channel (bankers' banks) and our product (sample audits plus a collateral tape) differ from the parent's per-head, borrower-facing, vet-split model. The competitors to test are traditional collateral-inspection and accounting firms doing agreed-upon-procedures work. They lack cattle-specific tooling and cannot reach a $400 price point without remote reconciliation.

title: Same-Week MFP Refunds for Senior-Care Pharmacies
one_liner: A refund-purchase facility for independent long-term-care pharmacies that becomes the payee of record on Medicare's negotiated-price refunds and pays out within two business days, underwritten claim by claim.
customer: Owners and CFOs of independent closed-door long-term-care (LTC) and senior-living pharmacies, and groups of 3-30 of them. First reached through the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition, whose members warned that 60% may close in 2026 without a fix. Our estimate, to be checked against real claims exports, is a float of $150k to $1M+ per LTC pharmacy (Eliquis, Xarelto, Jardiance, Januvia, Farxiga and Entresto dominate senior volume). That is 5-30x the $27k a month NCPA cites for an average community pharmacy, so each logo is worth far more.
problem: LTC pharmacies pay wholesalers full price on a 7-14 day cycle and then wait about 21 days (CMS/MTF average; 67% of NCPA respondents wait 22+ days) for the difference between price and Maximum Fair Price. They already carry slow nursing-home and PBM receivables. Their bank has a blanket lien and almost certainly treats a non-trade manufacturer refund as ineligible collateral, so the refund float is funded from owner savings or by cutting stock of the drugs seniors need. Merchant cash advances cost far too much for a stream that is statutory.
solution: 1) Onboard with 8-12 weeks of PMS claims exports and MTF remittance files. The free 'refund aging and dilution audit' is our underwriting diligence, not the product. 2) Make the refund land where we control it. Preferred route is being the pharmacy's designated payee, either as a registered third-party support entity if CMS and the facilitator allow it, or through a deposit account under a control agreement. That puts cash upstream of the wholesaler's weekly debit. Fallback is use-of-proceeds control, where the advance pays the MFP-drug invoice lines straight to the wholesaler. 3) Each week, score every MFP claim for dilution and buy the scored-eligible refunds at about 85% within two business days. The 15% reserve, net of our fee, is released when the actual MTF payment arrives. Recourse is limited to dilution through the reserve. There is no blanket credit recourse, and no 'non-recourse' promise we cannot keep. 4) Get the existing senior lender's consent or carve-out at onboarding, pitched as relief for their borrower's cash squeeze. Capital starts at $500k-$2M from a family office or regional bank, then a warehouse line from a specialty credit fund once 6 months of loss data exist.
why_now: The program has run since January 1, 2026 and the pain is measured and public (NCPA survey of 500+ owners, SCPC closure warnings). NCPA was still lobbying CMS on faster payment in September 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance, so no fix is in sight. On January 1, 2027 fifteen more drugs, including semaglutide, join and the float grows. The window is roughly the next three to four quarters, before a wholesaler or a bigger lender standardizes an answer.
revenue_model: Discount of about 0.9-1.25% per roughly 3-week cycle on purchased refunds (roughly 15-22% annualized), plus a $250 a month servicing fee per pharmacy. Illustrative unit economics for a pharmacy averaging $400k outstanding: $60-85k gross a year, about $36k cost of funds at 9%, under $6k expected dilution loss, leaving $20-35k contribution. Forty LTC pharmacies is about $16M outstanding and roughly $1M of annual contribution. An association endorsement, not Facebook groups, is affordable CAC at that revenue per account. Later, syndicate or sell seasoned receivables to a credit fund and keep servicing.
non_obvious_insight: LTC is the one segment where the parent's economics and its main risk both improve. Float per logo is 5-30x larger, so one association relationship replaces thousands of low-value retail leads. The dilution mode that worries everyone in retail, 340B lesser-of rejections, should be structurally small because nursing-home residents are rarely patients of 340B covered entities (verify pharmacy by pharmacy). The remaining dilution modes, discharge or death reversals and partial-cycle credits, are predictable from census and cycle-fill data that we ingest and a bank never sees. The lasting asset is a labeled dataset that maps each claim to its refund outcome. Interest is only how it is monetized.
first_30_days: Ask the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition for introductions to 20 LTC owners and run willingness-to-pay interviews, pricing against 8-12% bank A/R lines and 30%+ MCAs. Sign 5 pharmacies to a free 60-day dilution audit in exchange for claims and remittance files. Build the dilution model in a notebook from those files. Ask the MTF help desk and a healthcare payments attorney what payee-designation options exist. Have a fintech attorney set the true-sale purchase structure, UCC filings and state commercial-financing disclosures. Line up a $500k credit line from a family office or regional bank. Fund the first three advances at $25-50k each with a 25% holdback.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: We do not sell reconciliation. SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty and the free Beacon dashboards all compete on the report. Here the report is an internal underwriting input given away inside the advance, so there is no head-to-head feature race. Plenful targets health systems. Generic pharmacy lenders and Corporate Capital Direct advance against PBM A/R or MCA-style revenue and do not underwrite MFP refunds claim by claim. Live Oak's cheap SBA-style paper funds acquisitions, not a weekly refund float. We complement the senior lender through an intercreditor consent. The wholesaler's payment path, which the parent's research flagged as make-or-break, is handled by payee routing or direct invoice-line payment. That protects the wholesaler's payment, so it has no reason to object. Narrowing to LTC also sidesteps the small-float, high-CAC retail independent.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Paid Pet Claims
one_liner: A read-only shadow adjudicator plus a cross-carrier duplicate registry that independently re-checks every auto-paid pet claim against the policy's own clauses and produces the validation records state examiners now ask for.
customer: Head of claims and the compliance officer at US pet-insurance MGAs and small carriers paying roughly 100k-400k claims a year that already auto-adjudicate through a vendor platform or in-house LLM triage. The channel is the fronting carriers whose binders give them claims-audit rights over those MGAs. Narrowest wedge: MGAs that announced automation in the last 18 months and write in the 25+ states that have adopted the NAIC AI bulletin.
problem: Once claims are auto-paid, the insurer is accountable for the model's output but cannot see inside it, and the vendor selling the automation is marking its own homework. Two failures are invisible. One is silent overpayment: excluded lines paid (exam fees, cremation, prescription diets, supplements), wrong deductible, co-insurance, annual-limit or waiting-period math. The other is wrongful denial, which means complaints and market-conduct exposure. No single carrier can see the same PDF invoice filed with two insurers, or an altered invoice that looks fine in isolation. The parent's price-based edits add a third problem: reductions land on owners as balance bills, with no vet contract behind them, so mid-size insurers will not fund them.
solution: Read-only nightly export of invoice, policy form and adjudication decision, with no workflow replacement. (1) Normalize every invoice line to a canonical code (start from VeNom, so there is no taxonomy to defend). (2) Extract each policy form's exclusions, limits and waiting periods into clause-anchored rules once per form, human-verified. (3) Re-adjudicate independently and return agree or disagree per claim with a clause citation, sorted into three queues: likely overpaid, likely wrongly denied, and duplicate or tampered (PDF metadata, font and amount forensics). (4) Produce a monthly exam-ready validation pack with sample testing, drift and complaint linkage, which is what examiners request under the bulletin. (5) Cross-carrier registry: carriers contribute only hashed fingerprints (clinic, date, total, pet identity hash, line hashes) and get match alerts. Price benchmarks appear only as informational flags. They become a reason to reduce a payment only where the policy form has reasonable-and-customary language and the carrier opts in.
why_now: NAIC's AI model bulletin has been adopted by 25 states plus DC as of July 2026, and a 12-state examiner evaluation-tool pilot runs through September 2026. Under it, insurers stay accountable for vendor model outputs, and 'we cannot see the model internals' is not accepted. Pet premiums grew about 19% in 2025 on 6.98M insured US pets, and carriers are racing to automation (Five Sigma at Odie, Lassie at about 60% automated). LLMs make clause extraction from policy forms and PDF invoice reading cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Annual platform fee of $45k-$120k by claim volume (about $0.15-$0.30 per claim scored), including monthly exam-ready packs. Registry-only tier of $12-25k for small carriers and TPAs. Optional 15% contingency on documented overpayments prevented on contract-clear lines. Sales math, assuming a $350 average paid claim: a 200k-claim MGA pays about $70M a year in claims, so an $80k fee breaks even at about 0.11% of claim dollars. Month-12 target: 6 MGAs at $80k plus 6 registry-tier customers at $15k, roughly $570k ARR. The registry then extends to all US carriers at a per-lookup fee, an ISO-ClaimSearch-style utility for pets.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation has turned automation from a cost saver into a liability, and the vendors selling automation are structurally unable to vouch for themselves, the way an accounting firm cannot audit its own consulting work. Independence is the product, and it is a budget line that exists (compliance, delegated-authority audits) rather than one that has to be invented. Duplicate and tamper detection is the only kind of edit that gets more valuable with every carrier that joins and never requires fighting a vet or a policyholder. State anti-fraud immunity statutes generally permit sharing suspected-fraud data with anti-fraud organizations, which makes a hashed registry lawful to seed on day one.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: map which MGAs and small carriers have publicly announced automation, and list the NAIC-bulletin states each writes in. Recruit an ex-claims QA manager as design partner. Days 7-21: build the clause extractor on 10 public policy forms and the invoice normalizer on about 500 sample invoices. Days 14-30: cold-approach 25 heads of claims and compliance with a free 'exam-readiness shadow audit' of 2,000 of their auto-approved claims from the last 90 days. The deliverable is a one-page count of overpaid lines, likely wrongful denials and duplicates. Convert the best results to a $25k, 90-day paid pilot. Success is 3 signed pilots by day 90 and a registry seeded by those pilots' fingerprints.
lineage: mutation of I1056 ('Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany. | How this version avoids them: Five Sigma, Sirma, and Lassie's in-house engine are the thing being audited, so they cannot sell independent validation. Five Sigma also does not describe unbundling or benchmarks, and Sirma is a bespoke services shop. Trupanion is in-house and never a customer, and we do not target it. VetControl is German, built on the GOT statutory fee schedule, names no US customers, and cannot read US policy clauses. FairVet and Vet Receipt are consumer bill-checkers with thin data and no insurer audit trail. Verisk's ISO pet program covers policy forms and rating only, so it is a possible acquirer or channel rather than a rival today. VeNom and SNOMED-VET are inputs, so the moat is the clause-to-line rule corpus, the pooled fingerprint registry and examiner-accepted evidence packs. Avoiding price-based reductions removes the balance-bill risk that the parent's research flagged.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I found no dedicated competitor doing what this idea describes, and I could not check the many small RCM and consulting shops that a live web search would surface. What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. title: Mixed-Lot Calf Referee With Brix Price Formulas
one_liner: An independent, photo-stamped Brix grade taken at the broker's loading dock that turns a blind mixed-dairy calf lot into a formula-priced lot, so the best dairies stop subsidizing the worst and disputes get settled by schedule, not argument.
customer: Wedge: independent calf brokers and sale-barn aggregators who assemble roughly 200-800 day 2-7 beef-on-dairy calves a week from 10-30 dairies and sell them to raisers who have no history with any of the source dairies. Start with 3-5 brokers in one dairy-dense region. Second payer: the raisers who buy those lots. Not the target: contracted dairy-to-ranch flows and integrated operators, where source reputation already does the job.
problem: Mixed-source lots are priced at a lemons discount. The buyer cannot tell which dairy's calves are good, so he pays for the average and hedges for the worst, and good dairies subsidize bad ones. Brokers eat 'adjustments' and lose a buyer after one bad lot. When calves die at the raiser, the dispute cannot be resolved: the dairy blames luck and the raiser blames the calves. A raiser can self-test for $1, but the seller will not accept the buyer's number, and the buyer will not accept the seller's, so measurement alone settles nothing. Packers already apply standardized deductions for unknown health history, so that discount is passed back upstream to brokers.
solution: 1) Two techs sample at unload or loading: every calf in lots sold as 'graded', a 20-calf random sample in standard lots. title: Dairy-Backed Calf Guarantee Pool With Immune Screening
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of selling buyers a verification and later insuring the raiser, make the dairy, who controls colostrum, warrant its own graded calves for 21 days, with our grade as the price of admission and a reserve pool we administer, growing into a mutual or captive with an MGA and reinsurer behind it.
customer: Large dairies (roughly 1,000+ cows, which now sell hundreds to a couple thousand crossbred calves a year, a $0.5-2M line that they still treat as a sideline) that already run good colostrum programs (pasteurized colostrum, Brix testing) and are irritated at being priced at the herd average. First: 3-5 dairies in one region. Second payer: the raisers who pay a premium for guaranteed calves. Later: an insurer or MGA taking over the pool's tail risk.
problem: A dairy with excellent colostrum management cannot credibly say so, so it gets the average price. Buyers cannot underwrite the calves, and insurers cannot underwrite a raiser's loss because the raiser's housing and feeding confound the cause of death (the parent's own moral hazard problem), and federal Livestock Risk Protection excludes mortality and disease. Both sides distrust each other's numbers, and the grade alone still leaves the raiser holding the risk. The dairy owns the biggest early-death driver and holds none of the downside.
solution: Each enrolled dairy has every calf graded at day 3-5 by us. Excellent and Good calves get a Guaranteed tag: if a calf dies of covered causes (neonatal scours, sepsis, weak-calf, navel) within 21 days of delivery, the buyer gets a replacement or price credit up to the lot price. Claims are adjudicated by us using tag custody, necropsy photos or vet note and treatment log within 72 hours. Trauma and raiser-negligence exclusions plus a small buyer co-pay keep the raiser's incentives in play. The dairy pays a per-calf assessment into a segregated reserve we administer, priced by grade and falling as the dairy's grade mix improves, so fixing colostrum is directly rewarded. Poor calves are sold openly at a discount without a guarantee. Unused reserve is rebated at year end, mutual style. Stage 2 (about 50,000 graded calves): a licensed MGA with a fronting carrier and stop-loss reinsurance. Stage 3: a risk retention group or captive owned by participating dairies.
why_now: Beef-on-dairy volume is heading from about 3.2M toward the 5-6M CattleFax projects, at four-figure prices, so a dairy's calf revenue is finally large enough to fund a guarantee and its reputation is worth protecting. A published four-tier standard gives a shared, auditable eligibility rule. Packers already penalize unknown health history and the heifer shortage makes each lost calf expensive to replace, so buyers want risk transfer more than they want a certificate. Cheap custody capture makes claims adjudicable at a few dollars per claim.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf plus 15-25% administration and commission on guarantee assessments (assessments of about $15-30 per guaranteed calf, in line with an expected covered-loss cost near $15-20 on a $1,200 calf at 1.5% early loss, to be checked against real data), plus profit commission from the reinsurer and float on reserves. Dairy economics: a $35-60 buyer premium against a $15-30 assessment, so about $15-25 net per calf. On 1,000 calves that is a modest but real $15-25K a year. Mature sizing: 500K guaranteed calves a year is about $5M in fees and commissions, with a $10-30M revenue ceiling at 1-2M calves, if the pool becomes the industry standard. The moat is the dataset, the escrow role and the mutual's membership, not the refractometer.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is the cheapest credible signal there is (Spence): a seller who will pay if the calf dies proves quality without the buyer trusting any measurement. The grade becomes the actuarial rate table rather than a label, and dairies with bad colostrum programs are priced out until they fix them, which turns a data business into a compliance flywheel.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: sign 3-5 large dairies with pasteurized colostrum programs, plus one raiser or broker who will state a premium for guaranteed calves. Draft a one-page 21-day replacement-credit warranty (covered causes, exclusions, 72-hour claim rule, cap at lot price) and get it reviewed by an ag attorney, since a seller's own warranty is a sale-of-goods term but pooling across sellers may be insurance under state law. Open an escrow account. Days 15-30: grade and guarantee a 1,000-calf pilot with each dairy prefunding a $20 per calf reserve. Run the 21-day window and publish the claims ratio. Gates: claims under 80% of assessments and the buyer pays $35 or more a head over the ungraded price. If claims are high, reprice or drop the dairy. Stage 2 only after 50,000 graded calves and a signed MGA term sheet.

title: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense
one_liner: A $395, 48-hour kit for defense counsel that turns a letter-of-protection bill into line-by-line cross-examination questions and a signed rebuttal, with the testifying coder as the real profit center.
customer: Wedge: 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques in Houston-area and Atlanta-metro courts that take carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k. On those files a $3-5k billing expert usually needs carrier pre-approval or gets skipped. Buyer is the associate or partner running the file. Florida is a second-phase rebuttal product, not the entry market.
problem: Defense lawyers do not lose LOP cases for lack of a reasonable-value number. They lose because they cannot make the treating doctor's price, referral source and billing habits look bad on the stand. The billing expert is a $3-5k bespoke item, so on mid-size files it goes unordered and inflated bills get tried at face value. Claims examiners forward demand packages, often polished by plaintiff AI tools, without anyone able to read the coding. The parent idea sold a benchmark report. Florida's 768.0427 already gives a free Medicare-multiple benchmark, and hospital price files barely touch the chiropractors, pain clinics and physician-owned ASCs that do most LOP care.
solution: Order flow: firm uploads the LOP disclosure packet (letter, itemized CMS-1500/UB-04, records, factoring purchase price and referral facts where disclosed). Within 48 hours the kit returns (1) a line-item coded audit flagging unbundling, modifier-25 patterns, E/M level outliers and stacked facility fees; (2) a benchmark table with three anchors that are not hospital files: Medicare multiple, the same billing TIN's own negotiated rates from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files where it is in-network, and the factor's purchase price when disclosed; (3) a provider-bias sheet listing referral and ownership facts to ask about; (4) a two-page cross-examination outline keyed to specific bill lines for the treating-provider deposition; (5) a rebuttal outline against the plaintiff's billing expert, who will cite FAIR Health charge percentiles (the kit shows charges are what providers bill, not what anyone pays); (6) optional signed declaration; (7) optional testimony by a named coder-expert. LLM pre-codes the bill and a CPC/CCS reviews and signs in about 25 minutes, so marginal cost is roughly $40-90 per kit. Intake parsers are built for the structured demand packages plaintiff AI tools produce, so the plaintiff's arms race becomes feedstock.
why_now: Florida (2023) and Georgia (2025) reforms made LOP arrangements and amounts actually paid discoverable, and other states, including Texas, are fighting the same paid-versus-incurred battles. Plaintiff-side AI (EvenUp at a $2B+ valuation) is making bills and demands more polished, which raises defense spend on rebuttal. Payer Transparency-in-Coverage files give rates by billing TIN and NPI for free, and LLM bill extraction cuts coder time per file by more than half. None of this was workable in 2019. (Verify the current statutory status of each state before launch; I could not re-check because the search budget was exhausted.)
revenue_model: Kit $395 per file, deliberately set below the amount at which carrier litigation guidelines typically require expert pre-approval (verify the threshold in the first 10 calls). First kit free for each new firm. Signed declaration $1,900. Deposition prep $250/hr. Trial or deposition testimony $3,500/day. Panel-counsel program for firms or carrier panels at $3-6k/month for a kit quota. Target mix after 6 months: 12 firms at about 5 kits/month is about $24k/month, plus 10-15% of kits converting to declarations or testimony at 60-70% gross margin. Kits are the funnel, testimony is the margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is a testifying coder with a public track record in that state, not coder hours or a benchmark. Judges and juries reward a credentialed ex-hospital revenue-integrity director who has survived Daubert and cross before. Every deposition transcript, Daubert or Robinson ruling, judge and outcome the company accumulates becomes a compounding cornered resource (process power plus brand) that a carrier workflow vendor cannot copy by hiring nurses. Pricing below the pre-approval threshold is also a distribution hack. Counsel can order without asking the carrier, and the carrier sees the value afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-3: spend one day on the searches the parent's check could not run ('letter of protection billing expert flat fee', 'reasonable value LOP Texas Georgia') to confirm no flat-fee incumbent exists, then run 15 calls with defense lawyers to confirm the pre-approval threshold and how often the billing expert is skipped. Days 4-14: recruit two testifying coders (one Texas, one Georgia, ex-hospital or health-system revenue integrity, CPC/CCS/CPMA) plus 2 contractor coders, and one ex-panel-counsel partner as methodology advisor. Build the kit template from Medicare fee schedules and Transparency-in-Coverage files for the top payers in Houston and Atlanta, filtered to the roughly 60 CPT codes that dominate LOP bills (99203-99215, 97110-97140, 98940-98942, 72148, 73721, 62323, 64483, 64493-64495). Days 15-30: give 10 free kits on live files in exchange for a 30-minute review and a quote, then convert 3-5 firms to $395 kits and price the first declaration.

Starting in Georgia and Texas avoids Florida's statutory benchmark, and using payer and Medicare anchors avoids the weak hospital-file why-now.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget ran out before I could run any searches, so this is a partial check. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 URLs (the idea's cited sources, Maximus, PCG, PSI, Code for America, Kognito, Relias, Deloitte, Route Fifty) plus GitHub repo searches. What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats.

title: Vet-Verified Herd Exposure and Outbreak Index
one_liner: Rural large-animal vets sell two things from one app: borrower-approved, chute-side verified herd counts for ag lenders, and anonymized weekly syndrome tallies whose denominators come from those counts, giving lenders, insurers and traders a true disease-rate signal.
customer: Community banks and Farm Credit lenders (verified herd reports), livestock insurers and reinsurers, cattle analytics desks, packers and feedlot risk managers, animal-health company territory teams, and state animal health boards. Supply side is 25-50 large-animal practices.
problem: Lenders can't verify how many cows exist or where they are, and vets sit on that data unused. Vets can see outbreaks weeks before the state does but their tallies have no denominator, so a count of abortions means nothing without knowing how many bred cows are in that ZIP3. Vets also refuse to police clients, so neither product works if it feels like surveillance.
solution: One vet app and one relationship. At preg-check and weaning, the vet logs every head by EID or tag scan, age class, pregnancy status and location. The borrower approves sharing with a single tap, and the lender gets a timestamped Verified Herd Report. Every week the same vet sends a 30-second SMS tally by syndrome (abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths, respiratory, milk drops), aggregated with k-anonymity. Outputs are a per-1,000-head regional index for subscribers, a lender portfolio dashboard with a regional disease overlay, and later an exposure-plus-hazard dataset for livestock insurers.
why_now: Fall preg-check season is live now, so the first verified counts can be collected this quarter. Screwworm and other disease anxiety has traders, insurers and state boards asking for leading indicators. The vet-as-verifier trust position is the same in both products, so one sales conversation with each practice covers both.
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split about 50/50 with the vet, charged to borrower or lender. $500-2,000 per month lender portfolio dashboards. $2-10k per month institutional subscribers for the outbreak index. $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice on top of the per-head fee. Later, data licensing and pricing support for livestock disease cover.
non_obvious_insight: Verified herd inventory is an exposure layer, and vet syndrome tallies are a hazard layer, which is exactly what an insurer needs to price livestock disease cover. Neither layer alone can be underwritten. The denominator also lets the index read the 'absence of calls' signal properly, since call volume per 10,000 head falling during a quarantine looks different from a quiet region. Two revenue streams turn vets from reluctant borrowers' auditors into advocates: verification is borrower-initiated and tallies are anonymized, so the conflict-of-interest objection goes away.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 rural practices in TX, OK, KS or NE that each do thousands of head of fall preg-checks, and pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders via the state bankers' association ag committee. Run about 10 borrower pilots at $2/head with a form-based app and a PDF report. In parallel, start the plain SMS weekly tally with 25 practices and a free regional newsletter as the give-to-get hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against official confirmation dates and pitch 3 analytics shops for a $1-2k per month paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0338 + I0199 (Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders + Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning). Why stronger: Cow counts alone are a small per-head fee and the outbreak signal alone is a free-data-for-nothing pitch to vets. Combined, vets earn twice from one workflow, the outbreak index gets denominators nobody else has, and the herd data gains a hazard overlay, which opens the much larger livestock insurance and reinsurance buyer that neither product reaches alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.\n\nWhat the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.\n\nThe unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.\n\nStructural weaknesses to be skeptical of:\n- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.\n- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.\n- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.\n- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.\n- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Handoff Assay of Record for EU Recyclers
one_liner: A co-signed black mass assay with a stated uncertainty at each handoff from a first recycler to a hydromet plant, so both sides' EU Battery Regulation mass balances close. The regulated first recycler pays, on a compliance budget, not the seller in a settlement fight.
customer: First recyclers, meaning mechanical pre-processors that shred cells and modules and ship black mass on to hydromet. About 25-40 sites across the EU are in scope. The economic buyer is the head of compliance/EHS or the CFO. Secondary payers are the hydromet recycler, which co-pays for the input documentation it needs, and extended-producer-responsibility organisations that audit recycling chains.
problem: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 sets the calculation and verification methodology for recycling efficiency and material recovery. It was verified this session as in force from 24 July 2025, with annual data submission to the member-state authority from 2026 and first material-recovery targets due 31 December 2027. Secondary sources say it requires a mass balance of input, intermediate and output fractions with composition data, that black mass is an intermediate fraction, and that the first recycler must coordinate data across downstream treatment. Those points are not verified against the act text, and how input composition must be determined is unknown. Black mass therefore sits exactly at the joint. The pre-processor reports what it sent on, using its dispatch assay, and the hydromet reports what it received, using its receipt assay. When the two assays of the same lot differ by 5-15%, the chain shows phantom Co/Ni/Li losses or gains. The first recycler is blamed either way and cannot show whether it clears a recovery target.
solution: A Handoff Certificate per lot. A sealed sample-of-record is co-signed by both sites and assayed once by an accredited lab under a Gy-based protocol, with declared moisture basis and a stated sampling-variance component. Both sites use that single number. On top sits a Chain Reconciler, a small web tool. It ingests certificates plus mass and yield data, propagates the sampling variance through the delegated act's formulas by Monte Carlo, and outputs the documentation-format annual report. Recovery rates carry confidence intervals, for example 'Co recovery 91.3% plus or minus 3.1%, provably above target' or 'cannot demonstrate compliance'. The stage-1 recycler pays a certificate fee of EUR 350-700 per lot plus a EUR 25-60k annual site subscription. Stage-2 co-signs and pays a smaller receipt-side fee. Verifiers and PROs buy audit packs. Sampling is done by contracted crews with portable kits, so there is no station capex.
why_now: The first annual reporting cycle under the 2025 methodology is live in 2026, and the first 2027 recovery targets are 15 months out. That is when recyclers discover their handoff numbers do not reconcile. The methodology was only fixed in mid-2025, so any tool built for it is new. Black mass has also become a controlled, largely within-OECD flow (a secondary source cites Basel Annex VIII export limits), which makes a small, identifiable set of handoffs.
revenue_model: Subscription plus usage. Per-site ACV of EUR 40-90k for stage-1 sites, with lot certificates included up to a tier. Stage-2 receipt-side fees. PRO and verifier audit packs of EUR 20-50k. Ceiling of roughly EUR 1.2-2.7M ARR from 30 EU stage-1 sites, and more from hydromet co-pay and PRO packs. Later, recycled-content documentation for cell makers and OEMs, which phases in from about 2028 and needs verification, becomes a second, larger payer.
non_obvious_insight: The customer is not buying accuracy but consistency and a defensible uncertainty. For a regulator's mass balance, it matters more that both ends of a handoff quote the same number with a stated variance than that the number is perfect. A recycler at 91% against a 90% target cannot claim compliance without an uncertainty statement, and with one it can. The compliance owner has a different budget from commercial procurement, does not haggle over EUR 500 a lot, and prefers to have a third party on record. It is the same sampling insight, sold as risk cover instead of dispute settlement.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: read the delegated act's annexes and documentation template to confirm how input and intermediate composition is sourced, and kill or reshape the idea if it just accepts supplier-declared values. Days 5-20: ask 8 first recyclers for 12 months of black mass dispatch assays and hydromet receipt assays (both are on settlement statements). Run a free one-page Chain Gap Check that translates the assay gap into percentage points of reported Co/Ni/Li recovery. Days 20-30: convert 2-3 to six-month certificate pilots, and open talks with one environmental verifier or consultancy that would carry the Reconciler into its verification engagements.
lineage: mutation of I1326 ('Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SGS (independent inspection, sampling and assay), Bureau Veritas / Inspectorate (commodities inspection), Intertek (Caleb Brett / minerals and battery testing), Alex Stewart International. White space: Provisional, because the research was severely constrained: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any search ran, and the direct fetches of incumbent sites returned 403, 404 or no relevant content. Nothing below is web-verified. Likely unserved: (1) A sampling-variance-certified referee product, meaning a Gy/TOS-based protocol with a stated sampling variance, heterogeneity characterisation (variography, sampling nomogram) and a binding-settlement clause. Inspection majors sell 'independent sampling and assay' as a commodity service, but I found no evidence that they publish or guarantee sampling uncertainty for black mass. (2) On-site, containerised, inert-atmosphere sample prep at the recycler or gigafactory gate. Black mass is being pushed toward hazardous-waste treatment in the EU, which makes shipping bulk samples to distant labs harder. (3) Tying lot-level sampling data to EU Battery Regulation material-recovery and recycled-content documentation. The main risk is that SGS, Bureau Veritas/Inspectorate, Intertek or Alex Stewart already offer black-mass sampling and umpire assay and would call this an existing service. The whole wedge depends on their protocols being meaningfully worse than TOS practice, which is unproven and is exactly what the free duplicate-sampling study would test. | How this version avoids them: Inspection majors (SGS, Bureau Veritas, Intertek, Alex Stewart) issue certificates of analysis per party and commercial lot. I found no evidence of variance propagation, co-signing across a handoff or regulator-format outputs, though their black mass pages were only partly checked. Umpire work is a re-assay (Bureau Veritas page, fetched). Traceability and battery-passport software, which I did not research in depth, tracks mass and origin and treats assay as user input, and document-level verifiers do not measure. ALS and Alex Stewart supply the assay leg, and Multotec and Metso supply dividers. The seller-vs-buyer settlement fight where majors dominate is bypassed entirely.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed.

title: Implant Payment Index for ASC Networks
one_liner: Pool invoice-versus-payment data across physician-owned ASC networks to build the payer-by-procedure benchmark that only payers hold today, and turn it into the reference price index that carve-out contracts cite instead of each ASC's own invoice.
customer: First buyers are ASC management companies, physician-owned ASC networks of 5-40 centers, and state ASC associations, all facing payer contract renewals. Later buyers are ASC developers, lenders and PE sponsors building pro formas, and eventually payers licensing the index.
problem: Every carve-out claim hands the payer the vendor invoice, so payers hold the largest SKU-level implant price database in the country and use it in contract talks. Becker's July 2026 reported that this year's payer talks came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data. ASCs' invoices are trapped in AP, so each ASC negotiates knowing only its own numbers. Drugs have a public ASP benchmark, while devices have none, so carve-outs reference each ASC's invoice. Payers distrust that (invoice inflation, related-party distributors) and demand attachments, which creates the paperwork and the leak in the parent idea.
solution: Wedge product: the Payer Implant Scorecard. From de-identified 835s, case lists and a sample of invoices, per payer and CPT it reports the share of implant lines paid $0, realized payment as a ratio of invoice cost, markup actually realized versus the clause, and how the network's terms compare with peer networks. It ends in a negotiation memo with the dollar impact of each ask. Data is contributed give-to-get, and contributors also get a free carve-out lookback that feeds the recovery business. Governance: cells need at least 5 contributors, data lags at least 90 days, nothing is forward-looking, and outputs are ratios rather than vendor prices, with antitrust counsel reviewing the protocol. Then a quarterly published Implant Reference Index and a Model Carve-Out Clause (index plus X%, no per-claim invoice attachment). Later modules include developer and lender pro formas by payer mix and, eventually, a payer license.
why_now: Implant cost is the central ASC economics story of 2026 (Becker's, March and July 2026). Volume is moving to ASCs as CMS's CY2026 rule reportedly expands the ASC covered list; verify the exact list. Payers are using AI payment-integrity tools that will only get stricter on attachments, which gives them a reason to want an index. Invoice and contract extraction is cheap enough to build the dataset without armies of coders.
revenue_model: Networks pay $25-60k a year, or about $2-4k a facility a month, for the scorecard and quarterly refresh, plus a success fee of 10% of the first 24 months of measured implant reimbursement uplift after a renegotiation, measured on the same 835s. Data and pro forma licenses to developers, lenders and sponsors are later. A payer index license comes only once the index is a contract reference. Bottom-up: about 1,000-1,200 implant-heavy physician-owned ASCs at roughly $30k a year is $30-36M before the index and lender products.
non_obvious_insight: The information asymmetry runs in the opposite direction from what ASCs assume. Payers already hold the invoices, since ASCs have been sending them for years, but ASCs do not hold each other's. Because the deliverable is a ratio (paid divided by invoice cost) and not a price, it can be shared without breaching vendor price-confidentiality clauses. Once contracts reference the index, both sides drop the per-claim attachment process that causes the leak. A neutral index is also something an ASC-billing company or PM vendor cannot publish, since it would expose their own clients' leaks and their customers' data-sharing limits.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 ASC networks or MSOs plus one state ASC association, preferring those with payer renewals in the next 6 months. Week 1: offer a free 'zero-pay scan' that needs only 835s and a case list, showing the share of implant lines (L8699, 027x, C-codes) paid $0 by payer and CPT. Week 2: engage antitrust and health-privacy counsel to sign off on the data protocol and BAA/de-identification. Week 3: for the first network, add 20-30 invoices per top payer and CPT to convert zero-pay rates into dollars. Week 4: deliver the first Scorecard and negotiation memo for a live renewal, and sell a paid $15-25k pilot to two more networks. Kill signal: no network will pool data even under the protocol, or scan results show payers already pay implants at cost-plus almost everywhere.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I found no dedicated competitor doing what this idea describes, and I could not check the many small RCM and consulting shops that a live web search would surface. I also could not confirm Cloudmed/R1 or Experian Contract Manager features (the R1 URL 404'd). Both are plausible incumbents with contract modeling.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists. | How this version avoids them: Aspirion ContractIQ, FinThrive Contract Manager and Sift model one provider's contracts against its own claims. None pool implant invoice-to-payment data across many ASCs, and their buyer is hospital revenue-cycle staff, not ASC networks negotiating renewals. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways hold multi-ASC data, but as PM and billing vendors they lack AP invoices and contract clauses, and their incentives don't favor benchmarks that show client leaks. Consultants use anecdote and fee schedules. The moat is network economics plus a cornered dataset, and standard-setting via the model clause and index. Waystar, MDaudit and Aspirion sell workflow and recovery, and none of them are positioned to become a neutral price reference.
